A jinx is a person, object, or invisible force that is believed to bring bad luck — not just once, but repeatedly, in a way that feels like more than coincidence.

The most important thing to understand right away is that a jinx lives in the world of superstition and belief, not proven science. Nobody can scientifically prove that a person or object "carries" bad luck. Yet the idea of a jinx is very real in everyday human thinking, because sometimes misfortune seems to follow a pattern so strong that people feel compelled to explain it.

A jinx can take three forms.

A person. Some people seem to bring misfortune wherever they go — every team they join loses, every project they touch falls apart, and accidents seem to follow them around. Such a person is called a jinx. For example: "Don't let Kevin come to the match — he's a jinx. Every single time he watches us play, we lose."

An object. A thing — a painting, a ring, a car, a house — can also be called a jinx if bad things keep happening around it or because of it. For example: "That old clock is a jinx. Ever since we brought it home, something keeps going wrong."

An invisible pattern or force. Sometimes there's no clear person or object to blame, but bad luck seems to be sitting over a situation like a dark cloud. In this case, people refer to the jinx as an unseen force. For example: "There's a jinx on this project — no matter how well we plan, something always goes wrong at the last moment."

This is what separates a jinx from ordinary bad luck.

Ordinary bad luck is a one-off event — you miss your train, you drop your phone. It happens, it's over, and you move on. A jinx, however, involves a streak — a repeated pattern of things going wrong in a way that starts to feel impossible to ignore. It makes people say, "This cannot just be a coincidence."

Think of it like this: if it rains on one picnic, that's bad luck. But if it rains every single time a specific person attends a picnic, people start calling that person a jinx.

The bad luck a jinx brings is also seen as having a source — the person, the object, or the invisible force — which makes it feel different from random misfortune. There's something to point to.

One of the most common uses of the noun in everyday speech is in phrases like "that's a jinx" or "don't jinx it." This reflects a widespread superstition: if you speak too confidently about a good outcome before it has actually happened, you might attract bad luck and cause it to fail.

For example, if your team is winning a game at halftime and someone says "We're definitely going to win today!", another person might say, "Don't say that — it's a jinx!"

The belief is that premature confidence or celebration invites misfortune. The noun "jinx" here refers to that act of tempting fate — saying the good thing aloud before it's certain is itself considered a jinx.
How Jinx Differs from Similar Words

Bad luck is general and has no source. It just happens randomly. A jinx, by contrast, has a perceived cause — something or someone to point at.

A curse is more serious and deliberate. In stories and folklore, someone intentionally puts a curse on another person, often through magic or a spoken declaration of ill will. A jinx, however, doesn't require any intention — it just passively seems to bring misfortune along with it.

A hex is very similar to a curse — usually a deliberate act of magical ill-wishing, strongly tied to ideas of witchcraft. Like a curse, it implies intent. A jinx is milder and far more common in casual conversation. You'd use "jinx" in a lighthearted or even playful tone; you'd use "hex" or "curse" in a darker, more serious context.

A rough scale: jinx (mild, everyday, no intent) → curse/hex (stronger, darker, usually intentional).

"Break the jinx" means to finally end a long streak of bad luck. Example: "The team broke the jinx after 15 years by finally winning the championship."

"Put a jinx on something" means to be the cause of its misfortune. Example: "I think you put a jinx on the trip by saying nothing could go wrong."

"There's a jinx on something" means that something seems to be under a cloud of persistent bad luck. Example: "There's definitely a jinx on that corner — three different businesses have opened there and all three have shut down."

"She/he is a jinx" is the most direct way to call a person a carrier of bad luck.

Jinx is not a dramatic or heavy word. It belongs to casual, everyday conversation. When someone calls a person a jinx, they are usually being a little playful or light-hearted — perhaps slightly superstitious — but rarely completely serious. It doesn't carry the dark, threatening weight of words like "curse" or "hex."

A jinx (noun) is a person, object, or unseen force believed to be the source of repeated bad luck. It is not about random, one-time misfortune — it is about a pattern of things going wrong that feels too consistent to be coincidence. It lives in the world of superstition and everyday belief, is used in a casual and conversational tone, and involves no deliberate intention to cause harm (unlike a curse or hex). The bad luck simply seems to follow it, like a shadow.
